#840. Why KMI Panel frustrates referees too - and impacts their salary

Referees rely on the opinions of former players to determine a significant part of their annual salary

It has become something of a Wednesday morning ritual for fans. At 10am, the Premier League releases the latest votes of its Key Match Incidents Panel.

For four seasons, the KMI Panel was a clandestine operation. It was distributed to clubs only, but it would still find its way out into the public domain.

This season, it began being released to the public.

Yet little is really understood about the KMI Panel.

Why does it exist? Is it just protecting referees? And does it really mean anything?

For referees, the last question is more important than you might realise.

The votes, which ultimately say whether referees have got a decision right or wrong, create a merit table of performance - and this impacts their salary.

"It depends where you are on the list," former Premier League referee Graham Scott said. "But if you're in the middle, then it might be 25% of your take-home. So it's substantial."

For the officials, these are not decisions being taken by their bosses.

Their performance reviews are effectively outsourced to a group of former players.

The results can be inconsistent and frustrating as much for the referees as they are for the fans.

Let's take a look at how a referee's salary works in the Premier League.

A Premier League official will earn, on average, about Â£175,000 per year. The scale will run between Â£125,000 and Â£250,000.

Think that is unduly high? Referees in Spain's La Liga are the highest paid in the world, according to Marca, with an average yearly salary of Â£221,000.

Premier League officials are about on par with those in the German Bundesliga and Italian Serie A.

In England, there is a guaranteed base wage of 50%. This will differ depending on the seniority and experience of an official.

Michael Oliver would be at the top of the bracket, a newcomer like Farai Hallam at the other end.

The other 50% is based upon a set of variables, with match fees a major part.

Each on-field appointment is worth a little over Â£1000, with a VAR game slightly less.

Last season, Anthony Taylor refereed the most Premier League games, 31, followed by Chris Kavanagh, 30, and Michael Oliver, 29.

Kavanagh and Oliver worked as VAR on a handful of occasions, while Taylor did not do any.

Stuart Attwell had the most combined appointments at 52, with 25 games as a referee and 27 as a VAR.

Finally, there is the subjective element - the KMI Panel.

The votes determine the annual bonus payments for all officials.

Until 2022, referees' body Pro Ref, or PGMOL as it was known until this summer, used to do its own assessment of its referees' decisions.

But clubs grew restless, feeling referees were marking their own homework.

It is made up of five members. Three are former players and coaches, plus there is a representative for the Premier League and one for Pro Ref.

Their identities remain secret, with the former professionals selected from a pool on rotation.

What you won't see on the published version is that each incident is given a difficulty rating, ranging from one to five, which is taken into account when drawing up the referees' merit table.

All this really is, of course, is another layer of subjectivity. On top of the referees, VAR, players and coaches.

"People complain about the consistency of referees on field, of VAR interventions, or otherwise," said Scott, who now acts as the refereeing expert for the Athletic.

"But then, if you look at the KMI Panel outcomes, they're also inconsistent."

It is a view shared by Andy Davies, who retired as a Championship referee last year.

"Naturally, there will always be a level of interest given as it provides a significant part of income for the season," Davies said.

"But ultimately, the KMI Panel lacks any real credibility amongst referees."

Graham Scott was a Premier League referee for 10 years and acted as a VAR for more than 100 matches

Referees are scored on their on-field decision-making. If an error has been corrected by the VAR, it still counts as a mistake for the merit table.

Those at the top of the table will be rewarded well, while those at the bottom are not likely to receive much of a bonus payment at all.

Let's take a look at the numbers from last season.

Michael Oliver was the top referee, getting 93.5% of KMIs correct. John Brooks, Darren England and Simon Hooper were very marginally behind.

For other referees, the borderline decisions, ones which are the most subjective and sit in the grey areas, can be an issue.

One vote could be the difference between a referee being right or wrong. And a place on the merit table, impacting how much they get paid.

Last season, Sam Barrott and Jarred Gillett were both told they made four errors to a 2:3 vote.

Attwell, meanwhile, had three of the more high-profile incidents go in his favour to a 3:2 vote.

"The ones that sit in the margins can be very contentious and inconsistent," said Scott.

"You think, well, how can that be right? You know, that's not definitive, is it? It could have gone either way.

"But there seems to be a reluctance to allow that 'seen them given' sort of mentality, neither right nor wrong.

"Relying on such a small group of people to be so definitive, especially when they vote 3:2, is unhealthy and unhelpful."

As well as determining the merit table for each referee's salary, what the KMI Panel says can guide how games are refereed.

The members of the KMI Panel can be influenced by public opinion, and inconsistency means referees are often having to change the way they approach games, only to be told it is wrong.

"I have spoken to many referees, even this season," Davies said. "And they have no idea which way the panel is going to fall at times, or which way Pro Ref are going to vote because of how political it can be."

Scott used the example of holding when an attacker is offside.

In December last year, Brentford's Dango Ouattara was pulled back against Leeds. The penalty was cancelled by the VAR for offside. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was correct.

Last month, Arsenal were not given a penalty against Hull, when an offside Kai Havertz was pulled back by Nobel Mendy. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was incorrect.

"One minute we're told football expects an offside," Scott said. "Okay, we'll deliver that for you. We do it again, and they say the opposite.

"Referees get confused on the back of that mixed feedback. It just shows how the system's flawed.

"The game can afford to invest more in this process, and a properly independent approach."

For now, at least, referees have no choice but to rely on the KMI Panel to determine a chunk of their salary.

#838. Barbara Eden Reveals the Workout Routine That Keeps Her Fit at 95

I Dream of Jeannie’s Barbara Eden revealed the workout regimen she follows in order to keep her healthy and moving at 95 years old.

Barbara Eden does much more than think and blink, even as a nonagenarian.

In fact, at 95 years old the I Dream of Jeannie alum’s fitness routine includes more than those of some people decades younger than her.

"I go for about, I don't know, 35 minutes on the bike," Eden told Fox News Digital of her main exercise these days, which occurs on a stationary bike. "It's good."

And though she doesn’t go to the gym anymore, her previous routine involved “spinning class for an hour,” she explained, “and then I worked with a trainer for a half hour, lifting weights."

But she hasn’t completely put down the weights, though she doesn’t lift quite as heavy as she used to.

For Eden, staying healthy through fitness has long been a personal wish she’s happy to grant.

“You have to be disciplined about being active when you’re an actor," Eden—married to Jon Eicholtz since 1991—said. "My husband and I both have a trainer that comes in and helps us out."

Despite her disciplined routine, however, the Flaming Star actress can’t pinpoint just one source of her longevity.

Nevertheless, “I'm glad I'm here,” she said. “And I'm glad I'm still working."

She does, of course, try to make healthy choices—within reason.

"I'm careful about what I eat, but I'm not overly stupid about it, you know?" she said. "I've never smoked. I don't know if that means anything.”

As for skincare? While Eden emphasized using sunscreen, she said her own routine is only two steps: washing her face at night followed by moisturizer. As she noted, “That’s about it.”

For Eden, however, her philosophy about wellness goes beyond the personal and the physical, with external connection being a constant priority.

“I think one of the things that's most important in your life is that you recognize other people,” she mused. “You realize that they're not so different than you are and that you have to get along. And when you do that, you find life is much more interesting, and people are much more interesting."

For more stars who have lifted the curtain on their fitness routines, read on.

Eight months after welcoming her daughter Matilda with Tom Pelphrey, Kaley noted why she loves doing treadmill workouts amid her postpartum fitness journey.

"Putting that incline up is so good for your muscles, and for your circulation," she told Today.com in an interview published Nov. 22. "I'll also walk backward, which is amazing for your butt and legs. It pretty much works everything."

After having a transformative year in 2023, Becky revealed how fitness played a major role. "I know at the end of the day who benefits from a healthier me the most—myself," she told E! News. "Eventually, if you dedicate yourself to it, you will have lived your life longer with this habit than you ever did without it. At least, that's the way I like to think about it."

Her go-to workouts? "If it's a home work out, if it's stretch, if it's going outside for a walk—I try to be as consistent as I can be."

The Grammy winner explained how moving to New York City helped kickstart her health and fitness journey. "Walking in the city is quite the workout," Kelly told People in an interview published Jan. 3. "And I'm really into infrared saunas right now. And I just got a cold plunge because everybody wore me down."

Julianne told E! News the exercise she always blocks out time for when she has a jam-packed schedule.

"I know that I can walk around the hills with my dog," the Dancing With the Stars said. "That's key because I have to get her out, too. But movement in general, whether it's 10 minutes or five minutes of something, I have to move my body."

And when she has more time to break a sweat, she added, "Whether it's a Kinrgy class or doing Pilates or yoga, the fact that we get to combine all of those modalities is my favorite because I love versatility."

"I always move, even for a few minutes each day. Sometimes I'll go into a room, turn up the music and just dance. It's a great way to let loose and feel great."

The record producer opened up about his love for golfing and how it's helped him slim down.

"I do it every day and I get a chance to sit on the golf cart or walking about to answer an email or a call and handle my business," he told Us Weekly in an interview published Sept. 20. "It's so much [more] pleasurable, meaning [being around] the nature, the sun. It cleanses me."

"Honestly, my favorite way to break a sweat right now is playing VR. We got a virtual reality headset right as everything was shutting down and it's been AMAZING during quarantine. There are so many games that make you work up a sweat and it's so awesome. I am genuinely so sore after I play."

"Under normal circumstances it's going to the gym, but right now I'm taking online classes with my Pilates instructor Britni Lariviere. I'm also trying to jump rope—2,000 strokes each day."

"Family bike rides are big for us right now and I always try to carve out thirty minutes for pilates with Andrea Rodgers and foam rolling with Lauren Roxburgh."

Cardio kicks up your heart rate, so if you're not sweating, you're not working out hard enough!"

"I have been doing a lot of Sculpt, Cardio Boxing and Yoga Classes on the obé Fitness App and virtual classes with Pilates By Amanda. If I don't have a lot of time, I will do Lauren Gores' express workouts on her Instagram."

"During lockdown it's yoga under my own direction. I can go onto so many different tangents and by the time I am done it is often two hours."

#835. 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

In the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

#833. Calvert-Lewin signs new Leeds deal

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal until the summer of 2029 at Leeds; the striker joined the club in 2025 from Everton; he has scored six goals in all competitions this season; his form earned him a recall to the England squad

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal at Leeds, keeping him at the club until the summer of 2029.

Sky Sports News has been reporting that he was expected to commit his future to the club, which has now been confirmed.

Manchester United had shown interest in the 29-year-old.

Calvert-Lewin joined Leeds on a free transfer in the summer of 2025 after leaving Everton. He scored 15 goals across all competitions last season, and has scored six this season. He scored in a 4-1 win against Chelsea on Saturday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Since he joined Leeds, Calvert-Lewin is the highest-scoring Englishman in the Premier League (19) - three ahead of his next closest countrymen, Morgan Gibbs-White and Ollie Watkins.

His form for Leeds saw him return to the England set-up in March, and he also featured in the September/October and November squads. Calvert-Lewin was not selected for the World Cup.

Ao Tanaka is also close to signing a new contract with Leeds, Sky Sports News understands.

The midfielder is understood to have agreed terms on a deal that will keep him at Elland Road until 2029. The 28-year-old's current contract was due to expire in the summer of 2028.

Tanaka has grown to become a key figure in Daniel Farke's side this season, starting in nine of Leeds' 11 Premier League matches. They have lost just 10 of the 66 games Tanaka has started since then.

Calvert-Lewin follows in the footsteps of Ethan Ampadu, Joe Rodon, Jayden Bogle and Brenden Aaronson, who all signed new deals in the summer. Leeds are also reportedly set to trigger Lukas Nmecha's one-year extension.

Leeds are seventh in the Premier League, four points from the Champions League places. They face Coventry next in the league on Saturday.

Ahead of the weekend's match, Daniel Farke has refused to shed any more light on his own new contract talks. He signed a four-year contract when appointed in 2023 and that is set to expire at the end of the season.

He was reported to have parted company with his agent in October while reaching an agreement with Leeds in principle to extend his contract until 2029.

Farke said: "I'm the manager of Leeds United. I sign players. I don't sign managers. Since I've been here, I fell in love with the people here, and I fell in love with the club.

"And the only thing I care for is our supporters because they had to suffer really for such a long time. I want to bring success to them. I care for the players, I care for the staff and this is the way I work.

"I think this is also the reason I don't like to talk about my contract at all because I have to lead the people here.

"I'm a leader of men and women at this club and and no one wants a leader who talks about his future, about himself, or whatever. And this also not my style."

#832. The Mona Lisa Lottery

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gretchen Tessmer is an attorney/writer based in the US/Canadian borderlands of Northern New York.

There’s a bell ringing in the Underground.

The copper-line page phone in Shaft #4 is going off, but it takes a minute for any of the miners to notice. They’re too busy dealing with a tunnel collapse and subsequent break in the geothermal line servicing Sectors 51–57.

It’s late morning, as measured by the water clocks and those who swear by them. It’s midnight, as determined by the Moon and stars, cavorting a few thousand feet above their heads. But the oldest miner on this crew is 60, which is about 30 years too young to remember stars or moons, or appreciate the difference between morning and night.

This is one reason why the Mona Lisa Lottery, so loved by the old-timers, fails to stir up the same excitement it used to. Too intent on repairs, the miners forget that the annual drawing is scheduled for today.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Eventually, the ringing registers and curiosity calls them away from their work. Headlamps bob up and down in the dark. The sound of axes and drills drops off sharply, save for one stubborn miner still working, right below a rock face chiselled with the encouraging-but-long-false words: This Way Out.

They gather round the ringer box and the foreman hushes them before pressing the phone tight to one ear, cupping his free hand over the other. Every noise echoes tenfold in the tunnels, and the foreman has to ask the voice on the other end to repeat themselves.

“Abel?” the foreman repeats. “Are you sure?”

A few miners huff wry laughs at the name, muttering, “Of course it’s him.”

The foreman looks around, failing to find the lucky winner among his workers, “Well, where is he?”

A couple outstretched thumbs and jerks of the head give the foreman his answer, unmistakably directed towards the only pickaxe still singing in the dark.

No one can opt out of the Mona Lisa Lottery. No one can give away their ticket to someone else.

But Abel’s tempted to decline the honour. He’s got work to do. And climbing up 2,000 feet to wait in line with the other winners for hours, all to stare at a square 30-by-21 inches for 5 whole minutes, doesn’t seem like a good use of his time.

It’s only Adèle, the old woman in the cave next door, who convinces him to make the trek upstairs.

Adèle was ten when the evacuations happened. She’s now two months shy of being a proper centenarian. Her mind isn’t as sharp as it used to be. She can’t remember what she had for breakfast, but she remembers the horrors they descended from well enough, all those lines of desperate people sent down below with canned goods, heirloom seeds and not much else.

The treasures preserved from the Old World are few and Abel’s been given the chance to see one of the last. Arguably, the best. If she wasn’t blind as a bat, Adèle might kill him for his ticket. If she didn’t love him like a son, that is.

“Don’t be a fool,” she tells him plainly. “Go see what you’ve been missing.”

The journey to the higher levels snakes up ladders and through tight squeezes, skirting the underbelly of the Safe Zone. There’s a breath of strange breeze up here, not conjured by any air machines. It makes some winners too nervous and they abandon the wait, rushing back down the way they came.

Abel’s not afraid. But he still thinks it’s a waste of time.

Adèle warned him that the wait for the Mona Lisa was just like this. When she was eight, her family waited for two hours just to get a glimpse. It doesn’t make sense to him. He doesn’t understand how a mere painting could be worth the trouble.

He’ll never know. Because that’s not what the Mona Lisa Lottery is all about. Despite the name, Abel’s not queuing for oil paint on a poplar panel.

The Mona Lisa is not in the Underground. They couldn’t waste the limited space. Leonardo’s lady still sits in the crumbling ruins of her museum gallery, her half-smile gone grimmer these days. She’s lonely without visitors. A wild boar passed her way a decade before, searching for truffles in the jungles of the overgrown Louvre. No one’s been by since.

She sighs into her patient smile; she waits with folded hands. Ever the optimist, she thinks her friends may return someday.

#831. 'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith

Clinical Liverpool beat Brugge to return to winning ways

Liverpool fans have needed to be patient to see the best of Alexander Isak after an injury-hit start to his career, but the striker is now proving the wait has been worth it.

By scoring twice against Club Brugge in the Champions League, Isak took his tally for the season to 10 - more than double his total for his first season at the Reds.

Of course, that campaign was disrupted; he had no pre-season because of his protracted Â£125m move from Newcastle and then suffered a broken leg in December.

But Isak is now in a hot streak of form, having scored four goals in his past four games for Liverpool.

Asked whether fans were now seeing his full capabilities, Isak told TNT Sports: "It is always difficult to say exactly where you are and how good you are but I can definitely say I feel good, I am in a good place and the team is in a good place which is the most important thing.

Isak and Wirtz have proven their ability after last season - analysis

When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.

That meant he joined an exclusive club of just eight players to have achieved that feat, following in the footsteps of Dick Forshaw, Sam English, Gordon Hodgson, John Evans, John Aldridge, John Barnes and Mohamed Salah.

Isak has now scored the joint-most away goals across all competitions this season (eight â level with Erling Haaland).

His total is also already more than any Liverpool player managed away from home in the 2025-26 campaign (six by Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk) and it is only November.

Isak looks to be brimming with confidence, exemplified by his second goal as he latched on to a pass from Alisson to go through one-on-one and then chipped a confident finish past the goalkeeper.

But for Andoni Iraola, Isak's performance offered much more than goals, the Liverpool manager also praising the striker's overall contribution.

"He is in a great moment right now," he said.

"In the first half especially he helped us with the link up. In the second half it was more about defending a little lower."

Alexander Isak scored twice against Club Brugge but also showed a willingness to drop back and help link up Liverpool's play

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock agreed that Isak had shown he has more to his game than the goals.

"There were a lot of questions about Isak last year, about his price tag and what Liverpool paid for him," he said.

"There were a lot of people saying he doesn't take people on, but now he looks fitter and looks sharper and we are starting to see the quick, nimble feet again that we saw at Newcastle, with his nice touches and link-up play.

"So we are starting to see a different side of him. My big question in this system would be - can he press? Can he close down, can he affect the game in the other way that Iraola likes to do? Now we are starting to see that.

"All of it is coming together, which is great for him."

Isak and Wirtz in a 'good place' - Iraola

It is not just Isak who is looking the part in the Liverpool attack.

Florian Wirtz continued his impressive run of form with a goal that means he now has eight goal contributions in his last five games for Liverpool and Germany.

"Both are now in a good place," Iraola said of Wirtz and Isak.

"When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results everything looks a little better.

"The important part if they help the team to play well and get results. Alex and Florian right now are in a good moment."

But the Liverpool attack as a whole is looking dangerous, regardless of who plays along with Isak and Wirtz.

In Wednesday's 3-0 win, it was Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola who completed the front four, while in Sunday's 4-0 defeat of Manchester United it was Rio Ngumoha who played in Munoz's position.

"We have so many good players in our team," Wirtz told TNT Sports.

"Even when we can substitute some wingers, midfielders or strikers in the 60th minute or later it gives us a lot.

"It shows how good our team is and it is important for a top team to have a strong bench."

Liverpool's win against Club Brugge was their seventh from their last 10 games across all competitions.

"I spoke to Wirtz at the weekend, after the [Manchester] United game, and we were talking about his form - and he said 'well it helps that the team are playing well'," Warnock added.

"It's true because if you try to influence a bad team or a team that's not playing well, then it is much harder.

"With a fitter Isak, Wirtz looks a better player because now he is playing balls in behind that Isak is getting to, and getting in on goal on the back of.

"It has a knock-on effect, which is obviously like Wirtz said, he is playing in a team which is better equipped to suit him."

#830. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#829. Chelsea Q&A: Are Blues in crisis? What next for Fofana after viral interview?

Your questions answered by Sky Sports News' James Savundra on Chelsea's season, with Blues having lost three of last four in Premier League; Wesley Fofana’s unauthorised interview, the absences of Danny Welbeck and Estevao, and January transfer plans all addressed

After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.

As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.

Here, Savundra addresses Fofana's future, Joao Pedro's injury, transfer plans and much more...

Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.

James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.

Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?

James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.

Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.

You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?

The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso of Wesley Fofana: "We have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate. He has apologised. He knows it wasn't the right moment. The content wasn't right. "We are here to take things seriously and he said it wouldn't be repeated. We know it's something we don't want and they are not going to be repeated."

Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.

James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.

It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.

The fact that Xabi Alonso opted for a false nine in three matches prior to Leeds would suggest he believes there are shortcomings in both Emegha and Welbeck's games. It feels more likely that Chelsea will revisit the forward line next summer.

JD: How has Joao Pedro's injury affected how Chelsea has been playing as an overall team, and how has Xabi Alonso had to adapt to it?

James says: The stats are undeniable. Since the start of last season, Chelsea average 1.8 goals per game when Joao Pedro plays, compared to 0.6 when he doesn't. It's quite staggering the difference that the Brazilian seems to make.

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers look far more potent when they are playing off him. Danny Welbeck initially started in his absence at Brentford. However, he had virtually no impact and appears to have fallen down the pecking order.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

Xabi Alonso doesn't tend to give much away but he has described Emegha as being a player with "special" qualities. There's clearly an adaptation period required and Emegha missed a lot of football last season due to injury.

He was also signed prior to Alonso's arrival so it was very much a club signing. Chelsea's season has been derailed by the absence of key players such as Reece James, Joao Pedro and Moises Caicedo.

Alonso needs his big players to step up to ensure they can cope with the casualties - albeit to really key players.

Adam: Why does Alonso not start Welbeck whilst Joao Pedro is injured? Given his experience?

James says: The treatment of Welbeck has been puzzling. He performed really well in the opening two Carabao Cup matches of the season but has featured sparingly since the Brentford defeat.

It was interesting to see how late he was brought on against Tottenham despite Chelsea's need to turn the tide. The 36-year-old (happy birthday today, Danny!) clearly cannot get around the pitch with the same intensity and speed he did when he broke through at Manchester United but that was obvious when he was signed.

Alonso has deflected when asked about Welbeck's lack of minutes but perhaps his inability to press with intensity is one of the main reasons behind him spending more time on the bench than on the pitch.

He's still got a brilliant goalscoring touch - as seen last season at Brighton. He may benefit from more opportunities during a busy December period.

Tim: Should Chelsea be starting Estevao more often? If not, then what should we do with him? Where could we send him on loan if we can't guarantee minutes?

James says: Estevao has only started twice this season - both times at home. He made a huge impact on the pitch and on the supporters when he started in the win against Manchester United. His lack of physical robustness and defensive acumen would appear to be why Xabi Alonso has used him so sparingly.

However, I don't think his lack of minutes is going to be sustainable long-term. There's an argument given Cole Palmer's drop off that Estevao should get an opportunity at No 10. Chelsea see Estevao as one of their "untouchable" players and they would be extremely reluctant to let him leave.

I asked Alonso last month about whether a loan could be an option in January. The Spaniard said that it had not been discussed. Something is going to have to give at some point.

Estevao is still a teenager so has lots of learning and development left. However, he would be a key player for many of the top clubs in Europe.

He needs to find a way to force his way into Alonso's plans. A January departure is very unlikely but conversations will need to take place in the summer if his lack of football continues.

Saying that, if Chelsea do qualify for Europe next season then there should be more opportunities.

Sam: Which manager is in more need of a win on Friday, Oliver Glasner or Alonso?

James says: Both clubs feel like they are in very similar situations right now. Both signing managers to deliver a cultural reboot and sustained success. Yet both have had challenging starts.

I was at Glasner's press conference on Thursday and he spoke about lengthy conversations he had with the club owner earlier this week about January transfers and standards. Forest gave him an extremely lucrative contract and will want to give him as much time as they can.

However, given they have had five managers in the space of a year, it's difficult to predict anything at Forest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chelsea have full confidence in Xabi Alonso but home defeats against Spurs and Leeds have really harmed his approval ratings amongst supporters.

It would feel like a crisis if Chelsea lost three league matches on the bounce, so I would say Alonso needs a win just a little bit more than Glasner.

If Forest can create an atmosphere at the City Ground similar to their win against Manchester City then Chelsea will really be tested. Liam Delap will be desperate to prove a point.

#827. Leclerc denies having 'No 1 clause' in Ferrari contract

Lewis Hamilton, meanwhile, confirms they remain "free to race" after talks following their collision in Las Vegas, for which Leclerc was punished by stewards; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Charles Leclerc has strongly denied suggestions he has a No 1 driver clause in his Ferrari contract.

The Monegasque, who has been with the team since 2019 and signed an extended deal earlier this year, was speaking ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix as both he and Lewis Hamilton faced the media again four days on from their latest clash at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing a collision as he attempted to overtake Hamilton for sixth place in Las Vegas, with the incident also earning him severe criticism from Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur.

The Las Vegas collision came just three weeks after a fierce battle between the team-mates - with Hamilton running first and Leclerc second - on the opening lap in Mexico City cost Ferrari a likely one-two, with clear-the-air discussions required after Red Bull's Max Verstappen won that race.

Vasseur has hitherto played down the need to impose strict, pre-determined rules of engagement on his drivers to avoid future repeats. There had subsequently been speculation that, perhaps, there were contractual reasons on Leclerc's side preventing the team from formally intervening in this way.

But offered the chance on Thursday to address claims about the presence of a so-called 'No 1 driver' clause in his deal, Leclerc said: "I normally never disclose what I have in my contract, but I think this one is an important one to speak about.

"And I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract.

George Russell admits feud with Max Verstappen is 'avoidable' and 'unnecessary' ahead of Qatar Grand Prix

"It's never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc bore the brunt of Vasseur's post-race criticism last Sunday and, asked if he agreed with the Frenchman that the crash with Hamilton had indeed been "unacceptable", replied: "That it is unacceptable? Of course.

"As a team, we cannot afford to clash between team-mates and I think that is very clear for everyone. For the clash in particular of Las Vegas, as I said, I took responsibility.

"I think there's just tension around, that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future.

"That's all I'm looking for. But yeah, I do agree. It's unacceptable that both Ferrari clash together, of course."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Vasseur had promised further talks with his drivers following the race in Vegas, having insisted the clashes between the pair "cannot continue".

The drivers confirmed on Thursday that talks had taken place, with both the team principal and among themselves, with Hamilton saying they had been "good discussions" and "positive".

Neither driver said they would elaborate on the specifics of what was discussed, with Leclerc stating in the official FIA news conference that he "cannot disclose" what possible "solutions" were agreed to avoid future repeats or whether any restrictions were in place for the season's final two rounds.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton later confirmed they remained free to race each other this weekend in Qatar

"We're still free to race, and I think that's the ultimate goal of being here. We want to race, right?" said Hamilton to Sky Sports F1.

"Of course, we don't want what happened last week to ever happen, so we communicate. Charles and I had a good sit down earlier on and had our chat, and I I think moving forwards we can be fine.

"We literally focus on racing hard and fair, and continue to try and enjoy it. We do enjoy racing together, and we do have a really good relationship.

"It's obviously intense in the background, well on the outside, it seems a lot more intense than it really is inside."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton has previously called for the team to adopt clearer guidelines on how he and Leclerc are able to race each other but, speaking on Thursday, said it was Vasseur's final call to make.

"That's for Fred to decide ultimately," he said. "I made my point clear already about them.

"So yeah, there's not really much more to say on it really. I said my piece before and and my point hasn't really changed."

Leclerc and Hamilton are in their second season as Ferrari team-mates and will at least spend one more year in tandem in 2027, with the potential for more.

Asked if he thought they could move forward in harmony, Hamilton said: "I do. We're going to figure it out.

"We're team-mates at the end of the day and we do always learn from these experiences whilst maybe it doesn't necessarily look like it.

"There will be learnings that we take from this difficult period, and I still believe in everything we're building and working towards in the background.

"I came here with the goal of taking Ferrari back to the top and it has been a massively challenging season but it's so easy to look at the negatives but I like to look at the positives this year."

Ferrari can clinch the runner-up position to world champions Mercedes this weekend in Qatar and Hamilton added: "We are fighting for second in the Constructors' Championship, we have had wins, I think we've had the best car chassis-wise particularly this year and that's down to all the amazing people back at the factory who have worked and brought upgrades. I am so proud of them.

"Did we have the straight-line speed? No. That's something we are working towards for next year. If we are able to galvanise and improve on that section, we're going to be mighty next year in my view.

"I'm just trying to look at the positives, I think everyone seems to be focusing always on the negatives, which is obviously the easiest thing to do in life. But I try to remember the positives, and we've really done some amazing things this year together."

Hamilton added: "I like to think that we are stronger. I think that if everything was just great all the time I don't think you learn anything.

"When you're winning all the time as well, you don't learn a lot through that. You learn really through the hardest times, and these are the definitely very, very challenging times for Fred, for Charles and I, but these are the moments that you really learn and grow closer together, through conversation, communicating and having those sit-downs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc believes his off-track relationship with Hamilton is "really strong" and they now needed to find a workable way forward when racing each other on track.

"We're just really very much focused on trying to find a solution that works," said Leclerc.

"Particularly because I really believe we are in a good momentum and if next year we are to be in a position of fighting for the championship, it's even more so important to find the right solution for both of us to bring Ferrari back to the top.

"At the end of the day, we are two, one in each car, and we need to make sure that things just work out. At the moment, it's not working.

"Then, of course, I can take the blame from one episode and whatever. That doesn't really matter. It's just important that we find a compromise and a solution that works for both."

#826. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#825. Last chance to vote for BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting remains open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024

#824. Joan Smalls Says Tom Brady Was "Catalyst" for Candice Swanepoel Feud

Joan Smalls addressed her and fellow Victoria's Secret Angel Candice Swanepoel's friendship fallout, confirming that the South African model's new romance with Tom Brady was the reason.

Joan Smalls is strutting away from relationships that don't respect girl code.

One month after rumors emerged that the Victoria's Secret supermodel was unhappy with fellow runway star Candice Swanepoel for dating her former fling Tom Brady, she confirmed the New England Patriots alum was at the center of their friendship breakup.

"Unfortunately, that was the catalyst," Smalls said during the Nov. 25 episode of The Cutting Room Floor podcast. "I was seeing this person for a period of eight months."

E! News has reached out to reps for Swanepoel and Brady for comment and has not yet heard back.

Though Smalls doesn't consider Brady to be an ex, she clarified that they casually dated the former NFL star on and off between 2023 and 2024. Swanepoel went on to spark romance rumors with Brady in June.

And for her part, Smalls emphasized that before ending her and Swanepoel's 15-year friendship—which she confirmed took place in April—they were each other's confidants about love and heartbreak.

"You've seen the relationships, situationships and people I've dated, and I've confided in you in these spaces and we never had a crossover," she reflected. "All of a sudden, I stopped seeing this person, and three months later, you text me and say, 'Oh, we have to speak about something,' which is usually not a conversation we normally have."

The Puerto Rican-born model—who had confirmed their fallout in scathing comments under her own Instagram posts last month—had a feeling that Swanepoel, 38, was planning to name him her MVP.

"I called her and I asked her, I said, 'Is this about him?' She said, 'Yes,'" she recalled. "We spoke on the phone very briefly, and I was just perplexed and lost for words."

The confrontation was especially devastating because Smalls said Swanepoel—who was previously linked to model Andrés Velencoso in 2022—had been a guiding light during her romance with the Fox Sports commentator.

"She helped me write text messages to this person," Smalls, also 38, said. "She knew intimate things. Potentially to my detriment, I overshared. I was just being open with a friend that I thought was a safe spac

As for how the conversation went? Smalls accused her former friend of committing a cardinal girl code sin: Dating a guy your friend was romantically involved with.

"She came across as justifying her actions," she explained. "She started diminishing my experience to make herself feel better about the situation, which I think is what infuriated me."

Smalls believed that Swanepoel—who shares two sons with ex Hermann Nicoli—refused to take accountability for being a bad friend.

"It was this whole attitude of 'I'm an adult. I don't need permission,'" she posited. "Both are actually true: you are an adult and you don't need permission. But as a friend, you should consider me in your choices. Don't consider me in your apologies."

"Then she was like, 'Well, I'm sorry, but I'm going to explore this and so is life,'" she continued. "It was just this attitude of entitlement and lack of care towards someone who's your friend and something that I would never do to you."

Looking back at the conversation, Smalls felt that Swanepoel was looking to ease her own mind.

As she put it, "She wanted me to comfort her about her bad decision so that she didn't feel guilty by her choice and then she would constantly justify it."

It was especially difficult for the model since she prefers to keep her inner circle small.

"I rarely allow people into my life, and I'm very private," Smalls added. "So, if I let you into a space that I thought you would protect me as my friend, that's the only one thing I asked for you to do. Create a safe space for me to be myself, to open up, and you can't do that."

Following initial speculations about their fallout, Swanepoel's team detailed her perspective on their friendship.

"Candice has always been exceptionally private about her personal life, with her focus remaining on raising her children," her rep Amanda Ruisi told E! News in October. "She and Joan share a longstanding history and a friendship that Candice will always respect."

As Smalls and Swanepoel navigate life after their friendship, keep reading for more famous celebrity feuds.

The Sex and the City costars had dodged feud rumors for years, but they were reignited after Cattrall decided not to return for a third movie and made comments about her SLP that raised eyebrows.

"What was your reaction to Kim Cattrall telling Piers Morgan that you were never friends just colleagues?" Andy Cohen asked Parker on a September 2017 episode of Watch What Happens Live.

As she explained, "Just...heartbroken. I mean that whole week, you and I spoke about it because I was just...I don't know I found it really upsetting because that's, you know, that's not the way I recall our experience."

"So...it's sad but I'm kind of...I don't know, I always think that what ties us together is this singular experience is the thing," she continued. "It was a professional experience but it became personal because it was years and years of our lives. So I'm hoping that that sort of eclipses anything that's been recently spoken. That many years spent doing something so special that people had a connection with is such a privileged."

And though they didn't film scenes together, Cattrall did make a small appearance on And Just Like That.

During a 2022 TikTok challenge, JoJo Siwa described Candace Cameron Bure as the "rudest" celebrity, later explaining that she felt snubbed when Bure once refused to take a picture with her on a red carpet. Shortly after the dig, however, the Full House alum apologized: "I kind of broke your 11-year-old heart. I didn't take a picture with you. Ugh! I feel crummy, I feel—JoJo, I'm so sorry."

The two made amends. But months later, Cameron Bure was asked if she expects the Great American Family network, of which she serves as chief creative officer, to feature same-sex couples as leads in holiday movies. She said no, adding, "I think that Great American Family will keep traditional marriage at the core."

however, it seemed their hatchet was buried when Love replied, "Olivia - you're welcome. My favorite florist is in Notting Hill, London! Dm me for deets! I look forward to reading your note [winking face emoji]."

"So I just got to my dressing room and found this actual olive branch," Swift said in an Instagram video. "This mean so much."

Since when has lip-syncing been live? Sorry about that, but I think everyone who lip-syncs in public on stage, when you pay like 75 quid to see them, should be shot."

"When people show you who they are, believe them. I carry that [mantra] with me a lot. It has served me well."

So for somebody that don't have a child to like that comment? So many people want to say that party wasn't the time or the place, but I'm not going to catch another artist in the grocery store or down the block."

In February 2025, one day before the Grammys, Kanye updated his Instagram to follow only Taylor. He added no further comment, and his fellow musician did not respond publicly to the move.

#823. Carsley eyes Euros history with England U21s after draw

England Under-21s won Euro 2025 with an extra-time win in Slovakia against Germany

Lee Carsley has urged his England Under-21s to create a legacy as they aim for a third straight European title.

The Young Lions - who have won the past two European Championships in 2023 and 2025 under Carsley - have been drawn in Group A against France, Poland and co-hosts Serbia at Euro 2027.

Only Italy have won three successive European Under-21 tournaments - between 1992 and 1996 - but that was when just eight teams competed at the finals and not the current 16.

Head coach Carsley told BBC Sport: "The players I am privileged to coach and work with have a great opportunity to make history with three in a row in this format and create their own legacy within the under-21s."

He was speaking after Thursday's draw in Belgrade, with Serbia hosting the tournament with Albania.

"This group of players are in a really unique position and it will be a while before another group will be in this position," said Carsley.

"Let's go for it. Why not? Go all out to try to win it. That's what we're going to do. We have the players who can do that.

"They are highly motivated. We have seen that in the last two tournaments we have had, the players were so determined to win every game and it makes it a lot easier from a coaching point of view."

England will open their campaign against France - who they beat 3-2 in Bristol last week - on 16 June in Leskovac before facing Serbia in Belgrade on 19 June.

The Young Lions stay in the Serbian capital for their final group game against Poland on Tuesday, 22 June.
