#822. How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community

As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."

Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."  "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

#821. Bournemouth make European history after coming from behind to beat Celta Vigo

Celta Vigo vs Bournemouth. UEFA Europa League Round 1.

Estadio Abanca-BalaídosAttendance: Attendance20,002.

Report from the Europa League game between Celta Vigo and Bournemouth at Estadio Abanca-Balaidos; Iago Aspas put home side in front before Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan struck to earn the Cherries a historic victory as Bournemouth extended their winning run to 10 matches in all competitions

Bournemouth continued their magnificent run of form with a 2-1 victory against Celta Vigo, creating two bits of history in the process.

It was a club-record-extending 10th successive win for Bournemouth in all competitions, with the victory also marking the first time an English club have won their first five matches in major European competition.

Veteran former Liverpool striker Iago Aspas put the home side in front in style in the first half, before Bournemouth were reduced to 10 men when Bafode Diakite was sent off for a late challenge.

But Alvaro Rodriguez equalised early in the second half, with substitute Rayan coming on to score a late winner to give Bournemouth an unlikely win.

Bournemouth were fortunate not to go behind after 10 minutes, with an offside flag chalking off Pablo Duran's poke home from close-range.

But the Cherries fell behind 10 minutes later when record Celta Vigo goalscorer Aspas scored a screamer.

The 39-year-old had seen an overhead kick saved well by Michele Di Gregorio, but he picked up the ball on the right side of the area in the second phase of play, before cutting inside to curl past the goalkeeper and into the far corner off the post.

Things went from bad to worse for Bournemouth moment later when Diakite saw a yellow card upgraded to a red after a VAR check following a late challenge on Couhaib Driouech.

Tyler Adams replaced Justin Kluivert at half-time and the tactical switch drew an instant reward when Alvaro Rodriguez glanced home Amine Adli's cross to get Bournemouth back on level terms.

James Hill then drew a fine save from Ionut Radu - who is the only player ever to play for both clubs - before Di Gregorio was called into action at the other end to divert a long-range Aspas strike away.

But three Bournemouth substitutes combined for a late winner.

Adrien Truffert stole possession and broke before finding Marcus Tavernier the area. He laid the ball off for Rayan to sweep home and seal victory as Marco Rose's side made more history with a brilliant win at the Estadio Abanca-Balaidos.

#820. Taylor and Lewis suffer five straight defeats on Modus Super Series return

Phil Taylor came out of retirement to partner Adrian Lewis for England at Thursday's Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth, but the duo endured a disappointing return, losing all five of their matches; Taylor retired from professional darts in 2018

Phil 'The Power' Taylor and Adrian Lewis suffered five losses from five matches for England at Thursday's Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth.

Taylor, now 66, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after claiming his 16th and final world title. However, the 16-time world champion returned to action to partner his long-time friend Lewis for the tournament.

Their opening match on Thursday saw them face Scotland's John Henderson and Robert Thornton, with the England pair suffering a narrow 4-3 defeat.

Things failed to improve in their second outing, as Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-2 by Sweden's Andreas Harrysson and Anton Ostlund.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

A shock 4-3 defeat to unheralded Swiss duo Ansh Sood and Marcel Walpen followed, before Taylor and Lewis suffered a fourth consecutive loss, going down 4-1 to Germany's Daniel Klose and Liam Maendl-Lawrance.

Their fifth and final group-stage outing saw England take a 2-1 lead against Denmark, the only other side in their pool yet to record a victory. However, Ivan Springborg Poulsen and Andreas Toft Jorgensen responded by winning the next three legs in succession to condemn the English pair to a 4-2 defeat and a fifth straight loss.

Taylor revealed in September that the opportunity to partner Lewis was enough to tempt him back to the oche, although his return is not expected to signal a permanent comeback.

The 16-time world champion, who recently underwent successful hip replacement surgery, previously enjoyed considerable success alongside Lewis, with the pair winning four World Cup of Darts titles together.

The Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament continues in Portsmouth until November 28.

#818. Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A pregnant person with dengue speaks to a nurse in Peru, which has been hit by a surge of cases this year. Credit: Juan Carlos Cisneros/AFP/Getty

The debilitating viral disease called dengue has exploded in incidence far more than previously thought, a new analysis suggests.

The number of reported global cases of dengue, which is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, rose from 430,000 in 1990 to 14.7 million in 2024 — a 34-fold increase, the analysis says.

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

The data were presented on 22 November at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH) in National Harbor, Maryland. Scientists also provided some of the strongest results yet about a counter-intuitive way to curb the disease’s staggering spread: the release of specially modified mosquitoes. But researchers also presented discouraging data on other solutions, and scientists at the meeting emphasized that the campaign to beat back dengue will be complicated and costly.

“We’re in an extraordinary and pivotal moment” in the history of studying mosquito-borne illnesses, said Albert Ko, president of ASTMH. Trial results presented at the meeting showed, he said, that “we can get rigorous evidence on what works, what doesn’t and what needs to be done to scale these effective interventions to protect the 4 billion people” around the world who are exposed to dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses.

Dengue causes fever, headaches and severe bone pain. It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, a species of mosquito that thrives in warm, urban environments. Global warming and increased urbanization have expanded the mosquitoes’ range. Existing vaccines provide imperfect protection.

Cases of dengue are often recorded in disparate databases that aren’t easily comparable, says Ahyoung Lim, an infectious-disease modeler at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who was involved in the study on dengue incidence. The results have also been published as a preprint1 on Research Square ahead of peer review. This has meant that no single database has captured the total number of reported dengue cases over time, leading Lim and her team to compile the most complete record of reported cases and use statistical modelling tools to fill in gaps in which data were missing.

The staggering increase in reported cases isn’t surprising, says Eng Eong Ooi, a dengue virologist at Duke–NUS Medical School in Singapore, who was not involved in the research. Populations in urban environments around the world are steadily increasing, he says, which means that “more and more people are living at risk of dengue each year”.

One promising approach to curb dengue starts with breeding mosquitoes and deliberately infecting them with a bacterium called Wolbachia that reduces the insects’ ability to transmit viruses. When released into the wild, these infected mosquitoes pass the bacterium on to their offspring, eventually lowering the number of highly transmissive mosquitoes.

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

At the ASTMH meeting, another team of researchers shared results from the first randomized controlled trial in the Americas to test Wolbachia’s effect on dengue transmission. Between January 2021 and May 2022, the researchers released roughly 32 million Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes across designated regions of Brazil and monitored almost 6,000 children living inside and outside these regions. The children provided annual blood samples between 2020 and 2024, and the reseachers found that those in the Wolbachia regions were 68% less likely to be infected with dengue compared with those in non-Wolbachia regions.

These positive results mark an important milestone in proving Wolbachia’s potential to drastically reduce dengue cases, says Elisabeth Nelson, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health in New Haven, Connecticut, and a researcher on the trial.

#817. WWE’s Thea Hail Shaves Head on Live TV After Alopecia Diagnosis

WWE NXT star Thea Hail, the mentee of WWE alum Andre Chase, pushed back on the harsh beauty standards for female wrestlers during a Nov. 24 broadcast where she shaved her head.

As the WWE star called out how the sport's fan base puts undue pressure on its female performers "to walk through that curtain and be perfect," she shaved her head in an emotional display in the ring following an alopecia diagnosis in August.

"I'm sure you can all imagine how afraid I was to share with the world that at 23 years old, I was diagnosed with alopecia," Hail tearfully confessed during the Nov. 24 WWE NXT broadcast, "an autoimmune condition that causes you to lose your hair."

And the wrestler admitted that losing 40 percent of her hair in less than four months made her fearful about her future. As she explained, "I'd love to sit here and lie to you guys and tell you that I was super optimistic about this all, but I wasn't."

She noted that her new normal had her especially worried about how she would be judged if her hair never grew back.

"Since July, I've been asking myself the same questions you're all probably wondering," Hail continued. "Most importantly, 'How will other people look at me if I have no hair?'"

As such, her ongoing feud with WWE costar Chantel Monroe, who has frequently used Hail's bald patches as a part of their scripted confrontations on the program, has been difficult for Hail.

"Chantel gave me that answer really quickly, and she proved just about every fear I had to be true," she shared. "She made me feel so small and so defeated as a part of my life that I wasn't ready to share was exposed by somebody else."

In addition, she called out the beauty standard she feels gets held against women in the ring for looking anything from "too muscular" to "too skinny."

"Do you know how long every girl back there sits in the hair and makeup chair before they come out here just so you all don't tear them to shreds?" she questioned. "Because God forbid their extensions don't blend the way that you think they should, or their tan's a little weird, or you don't like their gear."

With that in mind, Hail aimed "to take this moment of weakness and turn it into a strength" to convey how her alopecia has become "a bit of a blessing in disguise."

Ultimately, the Pittsburgh native was all smiles as she ended her heartfelt speech by shaving off her mane with an electric razor while the crowd chanted her name.

Hail first shared her journey with alopecia in an Aug. 27 Instagram, captioned, "i now have alopecia areata… i have literally manifested going bald."

Emilia Clarke filmed battle scenes for Game of Thrones, but in 2019, she published an essay in The New Yorker titled "A Battle for My Life."Having a bad headache at the gym, "I reached the toilet, sank to my knees, and proceeded to be violently, voluminously ill," the actress wrote. "Meanwhile, the pain—shooting, stabbing, constricting pain—was getting worse. At some level, I knew what was happening: my brain was damaged."She was taken to the hospital for a brain scan."The diagnosis was quick and ominous: a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), a life-threatening type of stroke, caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain," the Emmy nominee added. "I’d had an aneurysm, an arterial rupture."Emilia had immediate surgery to seal the aneurysm, calling the pain "unbearable." While she was recovering, she continued, she experienced aphasia and was "muttering nonsense."A week later, "the aphasia passed," Emilia added, and she left the hospital a month after being admitted. At a 2013 brain scan, she learned a growth "doubled in size" and that she needed surgery again."When they woke me, I was screaming in pain," she wrote. "The procedure had failed. I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

Snoop Dogg's daughter Cori Broadus is grateful for her family.Because after she suffered a "severe stroke" in January 2024, her loved ones rushed to be by her side."I texted them that I just had a stroke and sent them a picture," she told E! News correspondent Will Marfuggi in December 2024. "Everybody just came to my rescue."Because of other medical concerns, Cori ended up staying in the hospital longer than she initially expected."I could have went home after my stroke, but my lupus wasn't doing so well," the Snoop's Fatherhood: Cori and Wayne's Story star continued. "My kidneys were failing. It was a lot going on."Today, Cori is on the mend."I'm doing great," she added. "I just had a little bit of motor skills that I had to work back on. But other than that, I was fine."

Shailene Woodley’s early 20s were not an easy time health-wise.“It got to the point where I was losing my hearing. I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

#816. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

#815. Eckert: Time to 'close the chapter' on Spygate ahead of Boro reunion

Tonda Eckert speaks to Sky Sports News reporter Mark McAdam about 'Spygate' fallout, their points deduction and reunion with Middlesbrough. Watch Southampton vs Middlesbrough live on Sky Sports Football from 7.30pm on Friday night; kick-off 8pm.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I think we've experienced a little bit more in the last 12 months than normal."

It may be the understatement of the century, but it's not a huge surprise considering Tonda Eckert is a relatively understated man.

The storm of 'Spygate' is over, but the aftershock is still being felt. Southampton are sixth in the table, seven points behind leaders Middlesbrough ahead of their reunion on Friday night - live on Sky Sports.

Were it not for the four-point deduction, the gap would be smaller. Were it not for the entire controversy, the Saints would possibly be in the Premier League right now.

Eckert knows he broke the rules, and is thankful for the club and the support-base for backing him. Something that wouldn't have been easy after the ignominy of being kicked out of the play-offs.

"There have been some points, especially over the summer, where I think the club has made a commitment that not many clubs would have made," he admits.

"I'm very grateful, first of all, for the opportunity to step up in the first place, but also for the support over the summer. Obviously, that goes from everyone in the building to our supporters.

Celta Vigo 1-2 Bournemouth: Rayan gets winner as Cherries become first English side ever to win first five games in major European competition

Brighton 4-0 CS Universitatea Craiova: Ibrahim Osman stars as Seagulls bounce back with Conference League win

Luka Vuskovic confident in Brighton's good form

Chelsea Q&A: Your questions answered on Wesley Fofana, transfers, Danny Welbeck, Estevao and more

"This summer has been the biggest test we can possibly have in terms of the relationship between a football club and a fan base, and a manager and a fan base. I think the supporters have been great. It's been a tough period for them.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Towards the end of last season, it was difficult to process for everyone because of the process we used. I would have wanted to address the supporters a little earlier, so it took almost two weeks before I got to speak to them.

"From there on, I think the commitment has been very clear. It started with the football club and some players who committed to the project.

"You could just sense, the closer we got to the season, that everyone wanted to leave that behind and show what we are about as a football club and how much joy we bring when we go on the pitch. We felt that throughout the summer and on the first day of training.

"To come out of that situation with new strength just shows what this football club is about. Now it's for us to look forward and make sure that we continue to do that.

"There was still some uncertainty for the first block of games, and you just need to find a way, for me and obviously for everyone else in the football club, to put that to the side. As soon as the season starts, you need to perform.

"Then, obviously, to close that chapter finally, we needed a decision from the club. I think that's helped us to close that chapter."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The uncertainty came from the FA investigation, which wasn't resolved until October. In the end he was given a fine and a suspended six-week ban.

"Obviously, it's never easy to work on a daily basis if you have some uncertainty, and that's not just for me," he says. "I think it's the same for everyone at the football club.

"But I think we found a way, even in the first block of games, to perform. There's always something going on in football, sometimes a little bit bigger and sometimes not as big, but you need to push that to the side and make sure you find a way to perform.

"Once the decision came, I think it was important for everyone that we could finally close that."

For Eckert and Southampton it is just about points on the board, now. Trying to make up the deficit they were dealt at the start of the season.

"Obviously, if you could choose, no one would choose to start the season on minus four points," he says. "That's what it is. I think we are strong enough to make our way forward in the table.

"You shouldn't underestimate us coming from behind. We've shown that we are able to chase teams down, and that's the job for this year.

"It's been important for us to get some points on the board early in the season. We are still not where we want to be towards the end, so we need to make sure we continue."

Last week, Southampton handed Eckert, still just 33, a contract extension until 2029. They clearly feel he is their man to get them back to where they want to be.

"I think we've always been very open with our ambitions," he says. "There's no point in hiding that.

"I think the conditions are there to go up. It's never easy, but it's for us now to finish the job."

#814. Sutton's predictions v Kings of Leon drummer Nathan Followill

Arsenal co-chairman Josh Kroenke should probably turn his phone off if the Gunners fall behind against Manchester City on Sunday.

Chris Sutton's predictions guest this week, Kings of Leon drummer and City fan Nathan Followill, is good friends with Kroenke - and says he will be in touch if the game is going City's way.

"I'm super excited for this weekend and I've got my smack talk ready for Josh already," Followill told BBC Sport.

"I've heard about the City fans with their inflatable bananas and I need to get myself one. My wife is going to be like 'er, an inflatable banana just arrived in the mail - do you know anything about that?'

"We are going to win 4-2 so I will be texting Josh throughout the game... and, after Erling Haaland's second goal, I will send him a picture of me kissing the banana!"

AI has also made its predictions, and you can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Followill got a behind the scenes tour of Etihad Stadium and City's training complex when Kings of Leon played next door at Co-op Live arena in 2024. "It's a beautiful stadium, and an amazing set-up," he said. "Their practice pitches are better than most college pitches in the US."

Followill has supported City for more than 20 years, external and his children have followed in his footsteps by becoming Blues, despite the best efforts of his next-door neighbour in Nashville, as well as Kroenke.

"When my kids were born, they both received a full Arsenal kit - head to toe - in the mail from Josh," he explained.

"Both times, they were returned to sender - instantly.

"My son and daughter are both City fans now, but my neighbour, Jeremy Connor, is Tottenham, and I mean flying the flag full on.

"When they lose, you can hear him screaming - and when they win, you can hear him screaming too.

"His son is trying to convert my son to Spurs and I am like 'that is never going to happen in this house!'"

Chris Sutton and Nathan Followill were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Followill says it was eye-opening to watch City's boys and girls' teams play when he visited their training campus. "I had no idea how much they put into developing kids from the youngest ages all the way up," he said. "That was probably the most impressive thing for me - to see how many young kids were out there, with the ultimate dream of pulling on that blue shirt one day."

Chelsea have scored and conceded 20 goals so far this season, which kind of sums up where they are at.

Xabi Alonso's side have also lost as many league games - five - as Manchester United, and United are in crisis.

Alonso is not under pressure, or anything like that, but if they lose this game too, you can imagine the mood of the club - and it won't be good.

Apparently their fans were singing 'you don't know what you're doing' at him after their defeat by Leeds - which is what they sang at me when I was there.

Alonso needs to decide on a shape and a way of playing, and stick with it.

Anything could happen here, because Nottingham Forest's form is hardly convincing either.

They tore Manchester City apart in their previous home game, before the international break, but can they really dig out another result like that here?

I think they will go about it in a similar way, and be aggressive and have a real go at Chelsea... and I don't see Chelsea's defence keeping them out.

Farke strengthened in the areas he needed to improve, but is still trusting some of the players who did well for him last season - the likes of Jayden Bogle and James Justin, who have been outstanding.

They are a really well-balanced team and they have good depth to their squad too. The only criticism would be that they are not usually free-scoring - they hit four against Chelsea but before then they had only managed 10 goals in their first 10 league games.

Leeds do not give much away at the back either, though, and I think that will be key in this game.

When I watch Coventry they are dynamic with their counter-attacks and I always fancy them to nick a goal like that.

Nathan's prediction: Coventry play in sky blue too? Part of the reason I became a Manchester City fan was the kit, and I have always gravitated towards teams in light blue, so I am going to go with Coventry here. 0-1

Brighton probably still can't believe they lost to Hull last week - but lightning is not going to strike twice.

Brighton should have buried them and I think Palace will get plenty of chances too.

Hull fans are probably wondering if I am ever going to predict they will win a game... the answer is no, at least not this week anyway.

Nathan's prediction: Palace have given up 27 goals in 11 games which is a lot. Hull have surprised a few people this season and I am backing them here. 0-2

Nathan's prediction: Both these teams have picked up a lot, so this is a tough one to call. 2-2

I love to see managers trust young players like that, especially because Spurs have had such a tricky season so far.

It will be interesting to see whether De Zerbi picks him again here, but I feel like the outcome of this game is more dependent on which Sunderland we see.

They picked up a good point at Villa last time out, but they never seem to be quite the same after they have played in Europe, like they are doing this week.

So I am going to back them in this one, because of Dave and also because of my neighbour Jeremy, who I mentioned earlier.

Somehow Maresca has got to find a way of nullifying Declan Rice, but that will be very difficult because Rice is just an absolute machine.

You can never rule City out because of Haaland's ability to score goals but the only result I see here is an Arsenal win, and I am going for a classic Gunners scoreline.

Nathan's prediction: This is the big one! It's huge. I feel really good about it, too. Arsenal are riding so high at the moment, I feel like we might catch them snoozing.

I predict Haaland will get two goals, Phil Foden will get one too and we will end up with four. 2-4

After drawing a blank since week two, Chris finally picked up another win in week 11 - and it was his spot-on prediction for Liverpool to thump Manchester United 4-0 that sealed the deal.

That meant he got three correct results, including two exact scores - at Anfield, and Tottenham's 2-0 win over Ipswich - giving him a total of 90 points.

In a tricky week for predictions, where Liverpool were the only team to start the weekend in the Premier League's top six who won, it was those exact scores that made all the difference.

Chris' guest, undisputed world champion boxer Lauren Price, the BBC readers and AI also all got three correct results.

But the BBC readers were the only ones to also get an exact score - in the Spurs game - giving them 60 points.

Lauren and AI both ended up on 30 points - AI did call Newcastle's draw with Arsenal correctly, but it was wrong about Bournemouth's win over Nottingham Forest, which everyone else got right.

Not many of you got that Liverpool-United scoreline correct, either.

From around 27,000 predictions, the most popular scoreline picked was a 2-1 home win and only 570 of you went for 4-0.

"When has AI ever gone for a 4-0?" said Sutton. "That's what the crowd wants. The crowd don't want AI - who wants mathematics?

"The crowd want gut-feeling and instinct. I think I should get 1,000 points for that prediction, because I was brave enough to go for it."

For the first time this season, there were SIX games where no-one made a correct prediction - who thought it was easy?

The biggest shock of the week was Leeds' 4-1 victory at Stamford Bridge. Again from around 27,000 predictions, more than 3,600 (14%) of you did back Daniel Farke's side to win... but just 11 of you saw that scoreline coming.

#813. Why Ezra Frech's Ear Was Bleeding During DWTS Finale

Dancing With the Stars pro Daniella Karagach explained why her partner Ezra Frech's ear appeared to be bleeding during the Nov. 24 finale before the duo took home the Mirrorball trophy.

Clinching the Mirrorball trophy was music to Ezra Frech’s ears.

Especially since the Paralympian had to power through an ear injury while taking to the dance floor on the season 35 finale of Dancing With the Stars Nov. 24.

The 21-year-old raised eyebrows when fans spotted blood on his face after his freestyle performance with partner Daniella Karagach—but it turns out he’d gotten scratched from one of her costumes earlier in the show.

“I’m so freaking sorry,” Karagach exclaimed to Frech in her Nov. 24 Instagram Story. “Are you OK though?”

Frech assured her that he was indeed “fine,” joking that the cuts along his face and his ear were just “battle scars.”

Still, the dance pro was mortified by what her costume had done, exclaiming, “Oh my gosh, your ear. Dude. My dress.”

The track and field star acknowledged that the injury was quite noticeable, adding, “People were like, ‘Your ear was bleeding when you were getting interviewed.’”

Karagach gave her partner one final apology before the duo took to the ballroom for the live finale, waltzing into the history books as Frech became the first amputee and the youngest man to win Dancing With the Stars.

But it wasn’t just a bloody ear Frech was dealing with, as his prosthetic leg accidentally fell off during his freestyle dance to Linkin Park’s “Numb.”

“The leg just wasn't on correctly, and I felt it,” he explained to Variety following the episode. “Sometimes it'll readjust and I'll be OK. And so, as I was running up the steps, I'm like, ‘There's a 50 percent chance my leg will resuction and I'll be OK.’ And that wasn't the case.”

Thanks to the quick thinking of pro Alan Bersten as well as Karagach, Frech was able to take a moment and attach his limb mid-dance before the pair got back in step with the rest of their routine. And Karagach was certainly grateful to have had that moment to reset.

“I was just like, there is no other place in the routine that he can do this right now, and he cannot do the whole routine on one leg,” the 33-year-old explained. “So, I was like, ‘Just put your leg on.’ And it's not like—we had one little trick in there that he did on one, like a 540. It was really impressive. It was really great. But nothing's better than him just clicking on his leg properly and continuing on with the dance. I was like, ‘This is our only shot to do that.’”

The moment definitely left an impression on the audience and the judges, as Derek Hough told the stars, “This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show. What you did tonight was forever. Kids will look up to you and see what's possible."

Fellow judge Bruno Tonioli agreed, adding, "What we witnessed tonight goes beyond dancing. This is a powerful, beautiful, life-affirming statement that will inspire the nation and the world."

#812. Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died

Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.

Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.

Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.

Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.

In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."

But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.

His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.

Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.

Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.

Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.

Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."

This article was originally written in German.

#810. Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed for First Time In History

Ahead of its 100th celebration, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed to Nov. 28 “in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators” due to a severe storm in New York.

If your Turkey Day plans include watching the parade, be prepared for some deflating news.

The annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in history, with the milestone 100th celebration being delayed two days until Nov. 28 due to a severe storm headed to New York City, an NBC spokesperson confirmed to E! News.

“Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided,” the spokesperson shared in a Nov. 25 statement, “in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, Nov. 28. More details to follow.”

Macy’s expressed gratitude for the many people who bring the parade to living rooms every Thanksgiving.

“Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year,” a spokesperson told MSNOW in a statement. “We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”

And while the announcement marks the first time the parade has been postponed since its debut in 1924, the Thanksgiving Day staple has been cancelled three times throughout its 100-year history—from 1942 to 1944—due to World War II.

This year, the monumental centennial celebration was set to take place on Thursday, when a coastal storm is predicted the Big Apple and eastern coastline, bringing rain and strong winds.

This poses a major safety concern not only for the millions of New Yorkers who watch the parade in person, but also for the thousands of performers who participate, alongside the nearly 30 floats and record-breaking 100 inflatables, which will include characters such as Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion and Hello Kitty.

And while viewers at home will have to wait a couple of days to watch the 100th annual Turkey Day spectacular in all of its glory, families will still have some parade entertainment on Thanksgiving.

As an NBC spokesperson shared, the network—which broadcasts the celebration—will telecast the 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 26 8:30 a.m. in all time zones.

#809. 'Laughing gas has ended careers' - so how common is it in football?

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16â24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

Does football have a nitrous oxide problem?

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

"So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

#806. BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount

BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.

Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.

BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.

CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.

German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.

BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.

According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.

German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.
